title: Maundy Thursday
hookLine: from mandatum, commandment: love one another, and many churches wash feet

lines: THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.
cards: An upstairs room in Jerusalem, evening. Supper is under way, Jesus and his disciples reclining at the table. Then the teacher stands up.
He lays aside his outer robe, ties a towel around his waist, pours water into a basin, and starts washing his friends' feet, one by one. In that world, it was work for a servant, not a host.
When he gets to Peter, Peter can't stand it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me."
So Peter, being Peter, swings the other way and asks him to wash his hands and his head too. Today's word is the name of that night.

teach.b: Maundy. The name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment.

teach.h: LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.
teach.b: Later that night, in John's Gospel, Jesus says: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another."
In Latin, that sentence begins with mandatum, and it became the chant sung while feet were washed.
And the commandment has a picture attached: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."
Love here isn't a feeling. It's a towel. It's kneeling, doing the job nobody wants.
Matthew, Mark and Luke tell what else happened that night: the Last Supper, when Jesus takes bread and wine and, in Luke and in Paul's letter, tells his friends to do this in remembrance of him.
Christians understand that meal in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood.

Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in them; other Protestants of a spiritual presence, or a memorial. Churches that share communion trace it back to this night. Some churches still wash feet on Maundy Thursday.
Popes have knelt to wash the feet of prisoners and refugees; in some churches, everyone takes a turn.
In Britain, the monarch hands out special coins, Maundy money, to older people each year, a faint echo of the old custom.

teach.h: A SUPPER, A BASIN, A BARE ALTAR.
teach.b: Then, in some churches, the altar is stripped bare. The night ends in a garden, with an arrest.

how: On Maundy Thursday churches in several traditions hold an evening service remembering the Last Supper, often with the washing of feet, and some end it by stripping the altar bare; some traditions practice foot washing at other times of the year as well.

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher is kneeling in front of you with a towel and a basin, about to wash your dusty feet. what do you say?

games.why: Peter refuses, until Jesus says, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." then Peter asks for his hands and head too.

practice: Think of your own home or work, and the job nobody wants: the dishes in the sink, the trash, the email nobody answers. Pick one, and picture doing it for someone else, without mentioning it.
If you pray, offer it as a way of keeping the commandment; if you don't, just notice what it's like to serve quietly.

wordCard.voice: Maundy. From the Latin mandatum, commandment: love one another. The Thursday before Easter, when some churches wash feet. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a commandment, from John 13:34. English maundy is usually traced to it.
